description: Sothmac Olarak Planet X ve SPHEREx görevi üzerinde çalışarak uzayı anlamlandırmaya yardımcı olmayı hedeflioyoruz.
summary: Sky Revisit is a free, public web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx observations into a time machine for the infrared sky. Anyone can pick a patch of sky by name, by coordinates or on an interactive SPHEREx sky map, then play its dated SPHEREx visits like a flipbook (blink), compare two dates side by side, or subtract them so that only what moved or changed brightness remains. Images come live from NASA's open archive (IRSA search plus HTTP range reads from the public SPHEREx AWS copy) and are aligned north-up and stacked per visit in seconds. Clicking any point shows its 102-colour 0.75-5 micron spectrum from the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky cube, and Gaia DR3 stars, SPHEREx quality flags and SIMBAD facts add context. We validated it: Barnard's Star moved 71.2 arcseconds between a 2019 CSA NEOSSat image and SPHEREx 2026, exactly what Gaia predicts. The site is live at https://skyrevisit.sothmac.com, open source and bilingual (English and Turkish), so students, teachers and amateur astronomers can join the search for moving objects such as a Planet X.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Sky Revisit is a public web tool for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. SPHEREx re-images the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, so every field already has a time series. Sky Revisit lets anyone open any patch of sky and see how it changed: play the dated SPHEREx visits as a blink sequence, compare two dates side by side, or subtract them (blue = earlier, orange = later) so that everything static cancels out and only moving or variable objects remain. This is the classic blink method that found Pluto in 1930, brought to the browser with real NASA data.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Find: the backend searches the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive (SIA2) for every SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 exposure that covers the field in the chosen detector band.

2. Read: instead of downloading whole images, it reads only the needed cut-out of each exposure from NASA's public SPHEREx copy on AWS with HTTP range requests.

3. Align: cut-outs are re-projected north-up, each exposure's own background (zodiacal light) is removed, and exposures are median-stacked into dated visits.

4. Show: the browser player offers blink, A/B compare and difference modes; every view is a shareable link.

Clicking a point reads its 0.75-5 micron, 102-channel spectrum from the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky spectral cube on AWS in 4-8 seconds. Optional layers add Gaia DR3 stars moved to each visit's date, SPHEREx's own contamination flags, and SIMBAD facts. An Aladin Lite map of the SPHEREx all-sky mosaic lets users pick any field. The five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, WISE 0855, epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) open instantly; any new field loads in 20-40 seconds.

VALIDATION

We found Barnard's Star in a 2019 CSA NEOSSat archive image and compared it with SPHEREx 2026: it moved 71.2 arcseconds, exactly the 71.2 arcseconds Gaia DR3 predicts. From SPHEREx visits alone we measure proper motions of 9.9 arcsec/yr for Barnard's Star (catalogue 10.4), 7.1 for WISE 0855 (8.2) and 4.5 for epsilon Indi B (4.7). The spectrum of epsilon Indi B shows the water and methane absorption of a cold brown dwarf.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

No installs, no code, no FITS files: students, teachers, amateur astronomers and citizen scientists can explore real SPHEREx data on any device, in English or Turkish. The next step is an automatic candidate finder that runs the same difference test across whole fields and lists sources that moved or brightened, as more SPHEREx epochs are released.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, fsspec, hpgeom, aiohttp, requests, Pillow, Matplotlib), JavaScript (vanilla ES modules, Aladin Lite), hosted on AWS EC2 with Caddy and Let's Encrypt. Code: https://github.com/kisakosemedya/spherex-blink

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES

Reading only the pixels needed makes a large archive feel instant; independent cross-checks with another spacecraft and Gaia keep the tool scientifically honest; a bilingual, mobile-friendly design makes it usable in classrooms.

Team Sothmac: Muhammed Emirhan Bukan, Tugce Meydan, Ahmet Hant, Kerem Can, Omer Kurt.
